This Open Space and Recreation Plan provides Winchester with a current report on the town's
recreational facilities and natural environment.  It discusses the town in a community setting, its
regional context, with sections on history, demographics, and growth.
Our open spaces and recreation facilities are significant contributors to the quality of life in
Winchester.  Our Open Space and Recreation Plan will present our historical narrative, our
community, its growth and development and the responses to it, and inventory of our
environmental and recreational opportunities, plus our goals and our plan to achieve them.
Winchester is highly developed but becoming increasingly inbuilt.  There is always a high
demand for access to limited outdoor recreation spaces and sports facilities.  Conservation areas
now used in their natural state, will be increasingly managed through forest management plans to
provide resilience to climate change, control of non-native species, and promotion of wildlife
habitat.  There is an increased awareness of the need to manage our ponds to provide better water
quality - biodiversity being the end goal of both efforts.
Since the last Open Space and Recreation Plan was approved in 2013, recreational facilities have
been upgraded and now support greater universal (ADA) access.  Digital trails maps are now
online to promote passive recreation in forested open spaces.
The Plan contains an environmental inventory and analysis, describing geology, soils, landscape,
water resources, vegetation, wildlife and environmental challenges.  It also includes an inventory
of lands of conservation and recreational interest, an analysis of needs, goals and objectives, with
an action plan for implementation.
It proposes controlled development or preservation of large parcels of open space, updates the
town's flood mitigation program; explores watershed management options; and deals with
conservation area management.  It describes recreational opportunities on playgrounds,
playfields, a bike path, and universal access.

2.A.  STATEMENT OF PURPOSE
This plan is intended to guide decision makers in understanding the importance of preserving
open space and recreational opportunities and to provide a vision for future actions that will
support sustainable development including environmental, social and economic growth.  Public
input has been a key component, which has included public meetings and input for various town
departments.

Its various sections include information regarding Winchester and its community setting, with
information regarding population and how that may impact current and future needs, an
environmental inventory and analysis, an overview of the town's natural environment, and its
historic and cultural features.
It gives information about the town in relation to its neighbors, so that regional and watershed
connections can be made, an analysis of need to guide future decisions, goals and objectives for
specific action, and an action plan, which provides recommendations to achieve them.

Its overall purpose is to guide us in protecting and enhancing our natural resources and
recreational opportunities, provide natural resource access and opportunities for all, and to
provide a vision guide us towards those goals.

2.B. PLANNING PROCESS AND PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
The Open Space and Recreation Plan includes contributions from the Conservation Commission,
the Recreation Department, the Engineering Department, the Commission on Disabilities, the

The Town of Winchester is a suburban residential community located approximately 8 miles
northwest of Boston, in Middlesex County, and encompasses an area of 6.49 square miles. It is
situated in a valley at the head of the Mystic Lakes. Winchester is bordered by several towns that
are suburban communities much like Winchester in size, population and character. These are
Woburn to the north, Stoneham and Medford to the east and southeast, Arlington to the south
and Lexington to the west.
The Mystic River Watershed has an area of approximately 76 square miles, encompassing 21
communities north and west of Boston. The headwaters are of Reading and form the Aberjona
River which flows into the Upper Mystic Lake in Winchester. The Mystic River flows from the
Lower Mystic Lake through Arlington, Medford, Somerville, Everett, Charlestown, Chelsea and
East Boston, before emptying into Boston Harbor.  Main tributaries to the Mystic River include
Mill Brook, Alewife Brook, Malden River and Chelsea Creek. The watershed contains 44 lakes
and ponds.  The Mystic River Watershed is one of the most densely populated and urban
watersheds in Massachusetts. Eight out of the fifteen Massachusetts communities "most
intensively overburdened" by environmental hazards lie within this watershed.
(Source: Mystic River Watershed Association - MyRWA)

The ridge of the Middlesex Fells, still largely covered by forest growth and containing three
large bodies of water, forms the eastern wall of the valley. Of these bodies of water, a portion of
the North Reservoir is located within Winchester. Northward the floor of the valley slopes
gradually upward to the higher ground in Woburn and southward towards the sea by the trough
in which lie the Mystic Lakes and Mystic River. (From History of Winchester by Henry
Chapman, 1936). The west side of town is hilly, rising towards Ridge Street, on the other side of
which lies Lexington.

sections.section_title: Winchester’s water resources and hills have attracted regional recreation for decades. The State
sections.content:
operates a public swimming facility at Sandy Beach on the Mystic Lakes.  Winter Pond, Leonard
Pond and Wedge Pond are frequently used for fishing, and Winter Pond is the town's ice-skating
area. Hills forming the Middlesex Fells have long been open to public recreation.
Originally an agricultural community, Winchester evolved into a mill town with the development
of the Middlesex Canal and the railroad. The late 1800's witnessed the development of
Winchester into a suburban community.   It is now a mature suburb, with easy access to Boston
via commuter rail and closely proximate to Interstates 95 and 93.

There is a goal to improve walking and biking safety throughout Winchester, connecting people
to parks and other natural amenities, in addition to preserving and improving existing open
space, street trees, water quality and natural resources.  This would include efforts to improve
water quality, (with improvements to stormwater discharges and water quality treatment to our
local ponds), invasive species management, and green infrastructure.

sections.section_title: 3.A.1.  Land Use: Winchester is a residential town, with the majority of land devoted to single
sections.content:
family homes, with some multifamily structures, apartments, and business and industrial.  There
is a small-town center, and no regional shopping malls.  There is a small industrial base.
3.A.2.  Transportation Networks: There are two major highways, Route 38 and Route 3.
Regionally, Route 3 provides a conduit running through Burlington, Woburn, Winchester and
Arlington.  It provides easy access to Route 60 and to Route 2.  Route 3 begins in Boston and
runs to the New Hampshire border. Route I-93, running just east of Winchester, provides easy
access to Boston and Cambridge.  The Boston to Lowell MBTA Commuter railroad line begins
in Boston and connects to the city of Lowell, with two stops in Winchester.  The Tri-Community
Bikeway connects Winchester to Stoneham and Woburn to the north and connects to the Mystic
Valley Parkway to the south, which connects to other bikeways into Medford and Cambridge.
3.A.3.  Shopping Centers:  Winchester has no shopping malls.  It has a town center with
opportunities for food, clothing, pharmaceuticals, books, barber shops and beauty salons,
banking, professional services, and restaurants.
3.A.4.  Agricultural Land:  Wright Locke Farm, on the town's west side, is a working farm,
sells produce to local farmer's markets, and provides raspberry picking, as well as "agroentertainment" during parts of the year.

3.A.5.  Aquifers: A small portion of Winchester located near Woburn’s Horn Pond provides an
aquifer for Woburn's drinking water wells.

3.B.  HISTORY OF THE COMMUNITY
Winchester was first inhabited by the Massa-adchu-es indigenous people, whose land was in in
an area north to what is now West Newbury, south to New Bedford, east to the Atlantic Ocean,
and west to present day Marlborough.  Sachem Nanepashemet and his wife were leaders of
people living along the Mystic Lakes, in what eventually became present day Winchester.
The first Europeans came north from Charlestown, who were granted land in 1630.  Much of this
land formed part of Woburn after that town was incorporated in 1642. Other Charlestown lands,
now part of present-day Winchester, were annexed to Medford in 1753 and to West Cambridge
(later called Arlington) several years prior to the incorporation of Winchester. Early settlement
was concentrated along Cambridge Street (Cambridge-Woburn Road) with some scattered farms
to the west and along Richardson's Road (Washington Street). Other areas settled before 1800
were located along the Medford-Woburn Road: Symmes Corner (at the intersection of Main,
Bacon and Grove Streets) and Black Horse Village (near the present-day Black Horse Terrace on
Main Street). Long before 1700, members of the Converse and Richardson families had built the
first mills in Winchester along the Aberjona River and for a hundred more years the area
remained purely rural. (Source: Winchestermass.org/communitypage) Winchester separated from
Woburn in 1850 and grew to be a suburb of Boston.
With ongoing growth, the town is developing a more urban feel, with the construction of large,
multi-family structures, although the downtown still retains a small-town atmosphere.
Winchester has many sites of historic interest. The town is a veritable museum of architectural
history, ranging from colonial to modern times, with a particular wealth of late 19th and early 20th
century structures. There is also a notable history behind many of Winchester's landscapes.
Though the town was once highly industrialized, several dedicated townspeople were influenced
by the parks movement of the late 19th century and initiated the town's transformation into the
attractive suburban "bedroom" community it is today. (Source: Town of Winchester Official Site)

The major employers in Winchester employ professionals in a variety of fields, most are private

The 2021 Massachusetts Environmental Justice Policy defines environmental justice as being,
"based on the principle that all people have a right to be protected from environmental hazards
and to live in and enjoy a clean and healthful environment regardless of race, color, national
origin, income, or English language proficiency. Environmental justice is the equal protection
and meaningful involvement of all people and communities with respect to the development,
implementation, and enforcement of energy, climate change, and environmental laws,
regulations, and policies and the equitable distribution of energy and environmental benefits and
burdens." Furthermore, the policy describes an Environmental Justice (EJ) population as, "(A) a
neighborhood that meets 1 or more of the following criteria: (i) the annual median household
income is not more than 65 per cent of the statewide annual median household income; (ii)
minorities comprise 40 per cent or more of the population; (iii) 25 per cent or more of
households lack English language proficiency; or (iv) minorities comprise 25 per cent or more of
the population and the annual median household income of the municipality in which the
neighborhood is located does not exceed 150 per cent of the statewide annual median household
income; or (B) a geographic portion of a neighborhood designated by the Secretary as an
environmental justice population in accordance with law."

3.D.1.  Patterns and Trends
Early European settlement was concentrated along the road from Woburn to Cambridge and
scattered upland farms existed in the western portion of town. The Middlesex Canal, opened in
1803, and the Boston and Lowell Railroad, opened in 1835, provided a transportation link to
Boston which supported small mills and farms along the Aberjona River. Later, manufacturing
and tanneries became increasingly important until the turn of the century when the railroad made
the town attractive for summer homes and to permanent residents. By 1900, parks had replaced
industry in the center of town and most manufacturing had moved to its northern portion. Around
the 1960's, the western part of the town was developed. Today's Winchester may be considered
residential and a part of greater metropolitan Boston. The farms are mostly gone, and very little
industry remains.
On January 13th, 2003, the Town of Winchester adopted a resolution establishing policy
regarding the importance of the preservation of certain properties in private ownership through
the use of Conservation and Preservation Restrictions.
Winchester is almost completely developed and due to the limited number of vacant lots. The
town is experiencing teardowns of smaller houses that are being replaced by larger ones or by
duplexes. There is a large increase in the number of homes being expanded. Some lots are now
scheduled for multi-family development.

sections.section_title: Zoning regulations preservation of open space and recreation is a value in current zoning
sections.content:
regulations which allow for Cluster Residential Housing. Cluster Residential Housing is allowed
by Special Permit in tracts of land consisting of 10 acres or more. The overlay allows for
maximum flexibility for developing land for single-family homes, open space, private
recreational facilities, and related off-street parking and landscaping. A minimum of 25 percent
for a Cluster Residential Housing or Planned Residential Development area shall be developed
as open space. Parking areas and vehicle access facilities shall not be considered in calculating
open space. A maximum of 40 percent of the Cluster Residential Housing site area shall be
covered by an impervious waterproof surface. Other recent and proposed developments include
multi-dwelling units on River Street, Cambridge Street, Converse Place, and Main Street.  As
these are primarily infill projects, their impact on open space should not be significant, although
the increased population density will put more stress on playing fields and open and passive
recreation areas.
The town purchased the entire Winning Farm property in 1999 to preserve the land and control
development. Over 27 acres have been preserved as open space and 12 acres has been developed
into town houses.  Approximately 65% of this land has been preserved as open space, some of it
with a conservation restriction, to be preserved in perpetuity.
(Source: Town Official Website)

The Pansy Patch, once open space of 10 acres has been constructed as a townhouse development.
The 20-acre area of Wright-Locke Farm remains dedicated to farming, with a conservation
restriction currently being planted as forest.
Winchester is a mature suburban community, now becoming more densely populated.  Little of
the town's original forest land remains, although it still retains protected open spaces as
conservation areas, parks, athletic fields and bodies of water, providing recreational opportunities
for swimming and boating.  Although density is increasing in the form of multi-family housing,
public open space has increased, pending the transfer an additional 16 acres, previously in
privately dedicated to conservation purposes.  Winchester contains almost 150 acres of
conservation areas, comprising 4% of its land areas, which does not include the state holdings at
Middlesex Fells at 287 acres (in Winchester, and the Upper Mystic Lake at 165 acres.

3.D.2.  Infrastructure
3.D.2.1 Transportation
Winchester has easy access to all parts of the metropolitan area via railroad, Routes I-93 and I95, and two state highways, Route 3 and Route 38.
Winchester's public transportation includes a commuter railroad line on the route from Boston to
Lowell, which provides daily, weekend and holiday service, MBTA bus service; and the RIDE,
also run by the MBTA, which is a transportation service for those with disabilities.
The Greenways Initiative is a series of shared paths that connects Winchester from the Mystic
Lakes to Boston harbor.  The Tri-Community Bikeway connects Winchester to Woburn and
Stoneham via a multi-use path.

Source: NSPC Priority Mapping Project Report May 2013
The MBTA is currently renovating the Wedgemere and the Winchester Center Commuter Rail
Stations. These renovations will bring the two stations up to date with the latest handicap
designs.

The town's drinking water is supplied by reservoirs located in the Middlesex Fells Reservation,
and by the Quabbin Reservoir in central Massachusetts. The town's water supply protection
program has been characterized as excellent, as it includes town and state ownership of most of
the watershed, watershed use regulations and a policy whereby watershed roads are not salted.
To comply with the Safe Drinking Water Act, the town has constructed a water treatment plant.
Other than restrictions on the use of water during summer drought, water quantity has never been
a limiting factor for town development.

3.D.2.3 Sewer Service

sewer system, which carries sewage to the Deer Island sewage treatment plant, located in the
Boston Harbor. As Winchester does not rely on septic systems, this has not been a limit to

3.D.2.4 Stormwater Infrastructure:
Winchester has a municipal separate storm water system (MS4), the purpose of which is to
protect public health, safety, general welfare, and the environment by controlling the adverse
effects of construction site stormwater runoff; post-construction runoff, and nonpoint source
pollution associated with street runoff.

According to the 2020 Master Plan, the town is looking forward to balanced growth, which will
expand commercial diversity and mixed-use development in the area of the Town Center, the
Holton/Cross Street area, along North Main Street, and the northern portion of Cambridge Street.
These new developments should offer entertainment and retail opportunities and prioritize
walkability to increase foot traffic to local businesses, accessibility to services and community
interactions, and create more compact development in some areas.  The housing should provide
more economically available options and a balanced mix of apartments, condominiums and

houses that can accommodate a variety of households, including large families, both young and
older adults, and people with disabilities.  It will encourage more commercial mixed-use and
compact development in areas that support economic vibrancy and areas identified as scheduled
for development opportunities.
A more densely developed Winchester will appear more urban but not necessarily affect open
space.  New developments will bring increased ecological benefits, as modern stormwater
technologies improve the level of water quality and control the quantity of water reaching the
river during peak flows.

Existing town playfields provide numerous opportunities for soccer, baseball, football and other
sports.  Parks contain tennis and basketball courts, as well as playgrounds for young children.
There is a skate park, a bike and pedestrian walkway through the middle of town, and a pond and

3.F. KEY OPEN SPACES
Key open spaces, such as the greenway along the Aberjona River, the Upper Mystic Lake, the
Town Common, the Middlesex Fells, and fields and conservation areas, play a very important
role, not only in recreation, but also in the ways they contribute to the beauty of the town. This is
especially evident in the charm of the Mill Pond Dam, located in the center of downtown
Winchester, and currently undergoing landscaping updating with the Aberjona Initiative.

sections.section_title: 3.G. THE KELLAWAY PLAN: A Scenic and Heritage Landscape
sections.content:
Heritage landscapes reflect the history and character of a place, are often created, and have
scenic qualities.  In Winchester, the Kellaway Plan has had a significant impact on Winchester's
appearance.  Kellaway created scenic ponds in the Aberjona River and connected them via
natural corridors.
"The beauty of the Mill Pond today is in large part due to the improvements that Kellaway began
in 1914: water rippling over the stepped dam, ivy covered bridges, and open, natural edges
accessible to the public and protected from encroaching buildings.  Indeed, photographs and
drawings of the Mill Pond that include Kellaway's bridges and stepped dam have come to
represent Winchester's identity." (Julie Khuen, Landscape Designer, from Architects of
Winchester, Massachusetts, Herbert J. Kellaway, Linking water, parks and parkways in the
Olmsted Tradition" 1995 Published by the Winchester Historical Society). Today, the Kellaway
Plan has been used as the foundation for the town's news landscaping plan, called "The Aberjona
Initiative", by landscape designer Juli Reimenschneider.

The ice age significantly impacted Winchester. The retreating glacier left a wide valley, kettle
ponds and granite bedrock forming hills in the east and northwest.  North to south topography is
generally flat, which contributes to periodic flooding along the Aberjona River, which flows
down the middle of the town between the upland areas.
The town has is currently engaged in flood mitigation projects and has signed a Joint Powers
Agreement among the towns of Arlington, Burlington, Lexington, Medford, Stoneham, Reading,
Wilmington, Winchester and Woburn, forming the Upper Mystic River Watershed Board.

(Source: Mystic River Watershed Assessment and Action Plan.)
In addition, Winchester participates with Reading, Burlington and Woburn to develop small
scale best management practices to increase stormwater infiltration.

A soils study was undertaken by the U.S. Soil Conservation service in 1964. The soils in
Winchester were grouped into three categories. They are:
a. Hinckley (droughty, sandy gravelly soils on three to fifteen percent slopes)
b. Hollis (rocky, shallow, very stony soils on three to thirty-five percent slopes); and
c. Charlton (well drained, very strong and bouldery soils on three to fifteen percent
slopes).

Henry Smith Chapman's History of Winchester, published in 1936, describes the town as
follows:
"The Town of Winchester lies within a pleasant valley at the head of the Mystic Lakes. The
eastern wall of the valley is formed by the rocky ridge of the Middlesex Fells, still largely
covered by forest growth and now one of the most picturesque parts of the beautiful
Metropolitan Park System.
To the northwest and west, the valley is enclosed by the tumbled cluster of hills which under
various names - Myopia Hill, Andrews Hill, Turkey Hill, Indian Hill and Zion Hill - stretch in
the direction of Arlington Heights and Lexington, by the rounded summit of Horn Pond
Mountain and the ledges of Blueberry Hill in Woburn. Northward the floor of the valley slopes
gradually upward to the high ground on which Woburn stands. Southward it is prolonged toward
the sea by the trough in which lie the Mystic Lakes and the course of the Mystic River.
There is an additional series of wetlands between the hills in the western part of Winchester
stretching from Whipple Hill in Lexington towards Sucker Brook, which flows into Horn Pond
in Woburn.
These features also result in ponds in the Middlesex Fells that provide some of the town's
drinking water.  However, the topography focuses stormwater flow and has resulted in flooding.

4.B.1.  Forest and Wooded Areas
In eastern Winchester, part of the Middlesex Fells Reservation encompasses approximately 300
acres and contains a combination of soft and hardwood trees. The Town Forest is located along
the town's southern boundary and is a 28.5-acre forest. The town's conservation areas are also
wooded.  However, most of the town is residential and not forested. As a result, the forested
areas are for the most part small and fragmented.  See

Forest and Wooded Areas Map
below.
Forest and Wooded Areas Map

Source: MassGIS Oliver

Winchester's significant landscape features include the Middlesex Fells, Mt. Pisgah, the
Winchester Country Club, Wildwood Cemetery, Wright-Locke Farm, Winning Farm and a
portion of Horn Pond Mountain. Winchester has purchased a portion of Wright Locke Farm for
preservation, and it operates as an organic farm, providing a link to the agricultural past.  Early
20th century landscapes, designed by Herbert Kellaway, are found along the Aberjona River. The
Mill Pond, a Kellaway design, is the focal point of the downtown.  In addition, Winchester has
many water resources that add to the community character including the Aberjona River and its
tributary Horn Pond Brook, plus the Upper Mystic Lake, and several ponds including Wedge
Pond, Winter Pond, Mill Pond, and Judkins Pond.  Some of these ponds provide spaces for
passive recreation, boating, fishing, and ice skating in the winter.  The viewscape of these
features is protected by Winchester Wetlands By-Law.

Significant Scenic Features Map
Source: https://www.mapsof.net/winchester-ma

MassHistoric Commission Inventory Map
Source: MassGIS Oliver

The Mystic River Watershed has an area of approximately 76 square miles, encompassing 21
communities north and west of Boston. The headwaters of the system begin in Reading and form
the Aberjona River, which flows into the Upper Mystic Lake in Winchester.  Leaving the Mystic
lakes the Aberjona River becomes the Mystic River and flows from the Lower Mystic Lake
through Arlington, Medford, Somerville, Everett, Charlestown, Chelsea and East Boston before
emptying into Boston Harbor. Other tributaries to the Mystic River include Mill Brook, Alewife
Brook, Malden River and Chelsea Creek. The watershed contains 44 lakes and ponds, the largest
of which is Spot Pond in the Middlesex Fells, with an area of 307 acres.
Mystic River Watershed Map
Source: https://www.winchester.us/165/Mystic-River-Watershed-Overview
Water for the Town of Winchester comes from the MWRA water system and town-owned
reservoirs located in the Middlesex Fells Reservation off south Border Road.  MWRA's water

comes from the Quabbin Reservoir, about 65 miles west of Boston, and the Wachusetts
Reservoir, about 35 miles west of Boston.

The water at Sandy Beach (fed by the Aberjona River) on the Mystic Lake is usually suitable for
swimming and is regularly used.  However, following heavy rains, these areas suffer from
pollution such as ammonia enrichment, low oxygen, habitat alteration and pathogens.
Big and Little Winter Ponds and Wedge Pond, have active neighborhood associations, which
work with the town to upgrade stormwater structures, and educate and organize to protect water
quality.  There are two small ponds formed by the Center Falls Dam on the Aberjona River (Mill
Pond and Judkins Pond) and additional small ponds in conservation areas.

The area around the north, middle and south reservoirs are water supply watersheds and
designated as a Zone A Water Supply Protection Area.  Zones B and C Surface Water Protection
Areas extend further out in the watershed and are also subject to drinking water protection
regulations.

Medford, with a small section extending into Stoneham.  Watershed lands and Water Protection

Flooding continues to be a significant problem. In response, Town of Winchester to develop a
coordinated approach to flood hazard reduction in the Upper Mystic and Aberjona basins. This
effort has led to signing of a Joint Powers Agreement among the towns of Arlington, Burlington,

4.C.2.1.  Aberjona River
The Aberjona River runs from north to south through the center of Winchester. It enters from
Woburn, winds through Davidson Park, forms Judkins and Mill Ponds and then flows into the
Mystic Lakes.  Open space and recreational amenities include a linear park system following the
river and The Tri-community Bikeway, which runs along the river.
4.C.2.2 Horn Pond Brook
Horn Pond Brook originates in Horn Pond, north of Winchester. Near the center of town, it
enters Wedge Pond then flows into the Aberjona River.  The Tri-community bikeway also runs
along Horn Pond Brook.
4.C.2.3 Middlesex Fells Reservoirs
Within the Middlesex Fells, partially within Winchester and partially in Stoneham, are several
water bodies that provide a portion of the town's drinking water. In addition, Long Pond lies in
the portion of the Fells that is within Winchester.  The reservoirs are surrounded by the
Middlesex Fell providing open space for passive recreation, with many trails for hiking.
4.C.2.4 Mystic Lakes
A portion of the Upper Mystic Lake lies in the southern end of Winchester. The southern portion
of the Upper Mystic Lake and the Lower Mystic Lake lie within Medford. The lakes are
controlled by the state Department of Conservation and Recreation and are managed as a
regional resource. The portion of the lake in Winchester features a public swimming beach.
Shannon Beach Playground offers a bathhouse on the beach and a playground near the beach,
with facilities for picnicking.
4.C.2.5 Leonard Pond
Leonard Pond is a man-made pond located between the Leonard Field and the Aberjona River,
and along the Tri Community bikeway. The pond is surrounded by a grassy area and provides
opportunities for fishing and ice skating.
4.C.2.6 Winter Pond (Big and Little)
Winter Pond, located west of the town center, is a kettle pond, formed by the glacier, and fed by
groundwater and storm water run-off. It is about 17 acres, comprised of two connecting parts,
and designated as a Great Pond. It is divided by a roadway into two sections, known as Big
Winter Pond and Little Winter Pond. The ponds are a year-round resource, used for fishing,
boating and ice skating. There is a small parking area along a portion of the pond providing
access.
(Source: Friends of Winter Pond Web Site)

4.C.2.7 Wedge Pond
Wedge Pond is near the center of Winchester and is fed by Horn Pond Brook, which in turn
originates from the Horn Pond in Woburn..  Elliot Park at the north end of Wedge Pond provides
access and recreation.
4.C.2.8 Western Hills Water Bodies
Smith Pond and Locke Farm Pond are in the western hills of Winchester, along with several
brooks and associated wetlands scattered throughout the western hills. These water bodies are
part of a greenbelt; large portions are contained within conservation areas and can be accessed by
trails.
4.C.3.  Flood Hazard Areas
The flood hazard areas, defined by the Federal Insurance Administration as having a one percent
chance of flooding in any given year, are shown on the Federal Emergency Management Agency
(FEMA) Flood Hazard Area Map, updated as of June 4, 2010.  For the most part, flood hazard
areas are contiguous to the Aberjona River and Horn Pond Brook.

4.C.4.  Wetlands
There are pockets of wetlands throughout town. The larger ones are in Winning Farm, Smith
Pond, Locke Farm, Sachem Swamp and Sucker Book Conservation Areas. There are smaller
areas that border streams and creeks, as well as wetlands formed by the Aberjona River.

4.D.1. General Inventory
Herbaceous plants common to Winchester conservation spaces include flowering types, such as
Asters, Bellwort, Canada Mayflower, Cinquefoil, Goldenrod, Indian Pipe, Jack-in-the-Pulpit,
Loosestrife, Pink Lady slipper, Sarsaparilla, Skunk Cabbage, Solomon Plume, Spotted
Wintergreen, Swamp Buttercup, Turtlehead, Wild Geranium and various ferns.  Since

Winchester is largely built-out suburban community, most of the vegetation is cultivated
landscape on private property. (See also Appendix G: Guide to Winchester Woodlands)

Wooded areas in Winchester are concentrated in the eastern and western parts of town, with the
central valley around the Aberjona River being developed and sparsely wooded. In the east, the
Middlesex Fells Reservation, managed by the Department of Conservation and Recreation,
contains soft and hardwood trees with hardwood predominating. There are small patches of
hardwoods within the northeastern section of town outside the Fells area. Scattered small stands
of hardwoods exist in Winchester's central valley, along the Aberjona River and the Horn Pond

Brook. The Town Forest, managed by the Conservation Commission, encompasses 28.5 acres of
hardwood trees along the town's southern boundary.  These forested areas are used for passive
recreation, for wetlands protection and to provide habitat for biodiversity. The Winchester Town
Cemetery is also heavily wooded.
Specific types of trees include oak, hickory, maple, birch, beech, black cherry, hemlocks,
willows, pines, hop hornbeam, sassafras and ash.

These forested areas are used for passive recreation, for wetlands protection and to provide
habitat for biodiversity.

The Conservation Commission also funds a wildlife habitat replacement program, funded by
requiring tree replacements for those trees removed under a Commission permit.

The Select Board has established a Permanent Street Tree Committee to assist the town in the
planning, funding, and implementation of street-tree planting and maintenance. The Committee
is an advisory committee, which provides policy recommendations to the Board of Selectmen,
Planning Board and Capital Planning Committee and assists in the annual determination of
funding to contribute to the goal of the "greening of Winchester."  It provides local guidance on
tree planting, maintenance and removal as well as other administrative elements of Winchester's

Street Tree planting programs.  These trees improve air quality, provide glare and heat
protection, reduce noise, aid in the stabilization of soil, provide natural flood-and climate-control
properties, contribute habitats and provide food for wildlife, enhance property values, provide
natural privacy to neighbors, and absorb carbon dioxide and return oxygen to the atmosphere.
Winchester is recognized by the National Arbor Day Foundation as a Tree City USA Community
for its ongoing efforts to maintain and improve the quality of life through its Street Tree

Winchester maintains a street tree program, and plants about 40 trees annually.  This program is
funded by the Peter Van Aken Street Tree fund, and from annual appropriations for the planting,
care and maintenance of street trees.

4.E.1.  Inventory
Winchester is host to deer, and small mammal species such as raccoon, woodchuck, muskrat,
skunk, rabbit, squirrel, chipmunk, turkey, and fox. Aside from the special attraction of

Winchester’s water bodies to waterfowl, the bird population is diverse and common to this area.
As with many areas along the eastern seaboard, Winchester has become a permanent home to
Canada Geese.  Predatory birds, such as osprey, hawk and bald eagles have been increasing.

The Aberjona River and the Horn Pond Brook, the town's main waterways, form two green
belts, with natural vegetation that allow wildlife to migrate from one habitat to another. The
Middlesex Fells in the eastern portion of town, as well as Smith Pond and Locke Farm, Sachem
Swamp, the Science Park at the Vinson-Owens School, and Sucker Brook in the western portion
serve as wildlife corridors.  Fish ladders have been installed at the Mystic Lake Dam, the Center
Falls Dam in Winchester, and at Horn Pond in Woburn.  A daylighted culvert has been added to
Skillings Field in Winchester, enabling a large herring migration from Boston Harbor to Horn
Pond in Woburn, and up the Aberjona River from Winchester to Woburn and to headwaters in
Reading.  See below for herring migration statistics.

Source: Mystic River Watershed Association:  Mysticriver.org/herring-monitoring.

Ludwigia polycarpa (many fruited false loosestrife) Asclepias verticillata
(Linear leaved milkweed), Panicum philadelphium (Philadelphia panic grass)
and Arabis missouriensis (green rock cress).   Several plants on the state's watch list have
also been found Lipocarpa micrantha (dwarf bulrush), which may soon be listed, also
occurs in Winchester.
Fauna: Blanding's turtle, the spotted turtle, bald eagles.
These species are found in two areas: Winter Pond and Horn Pond Mountain (see map

4.F. SCENIC RESOURCES AND UNIQUE ENVIRONMENTS
Winchester contains notable landscapes in Mt. Pisgah, portions of Horn Pond Mountain and the

Kellaway Greenway along the Aberjona River. Other scenic views include Judkins Pond, Wedge
Pond, Mill Pond, the Mystic Lakes and the Middlesex Fells. The Mystic Valley Parkway, which
runs through Winchester, is also considered a scenic landscape.  The Town Forest and the

sections.section_title: Middlesex Fells are large tracts of mature forest for residents to enjoy.
sections.content:
Recognizing the importance of Winchester's ponds and streams, in 1910 the town hired a Boston
landscape architect, Herbert J. Kellaway, to recommend ways to improve the town's waterways
which had become badly polluted.  His ideas of preserving open space for public use and
connecting those spaces through green corridors greatly affected Winchester's appearance today.
The beauty of Mill Pond is due in large part to the improvements Kellaway began in 1914: Water
rippling over the stepped dam, ivy covered bridges and open natural edges accessible to the
public and protected from encroaching buildings. Indeed, photographs and drawings of the Mill
Pond that include Kellaway's bridges and stepped dam have come to represent Winchester's
identity.
(Source: The Architecture of Winchester, MA, by Julie Kheun)
In 2015 the Town started the Aberjona Initiative to restore a healthy, sustainable and beautiful
habitat along the banks of the downtown waterways, and to provide a foundation for: cultural
displays and events, resident and visitor enjoyment, commercial and business events, and town
gatherings.  The Landscape Plan for the Initiative includes removal of overgrown and invasive
plants to restore visual and physical access to the waterway and planting of native species to
provide wildlife habitat and visual interest and enjoyment for visitors.  The effort is ongoing with
the goal of establishing a Riverwalk in Winchester.
The Town Common is the site of community activities such as Town Day, Art in the Park, and
Concerts on the Common. It provides an open space of natural beauty within the civic center.
In addition, it has a beautiful old oak tree in the middle of the Common, which provides a
wonderful gathering spot.
The Wildwood Cemetery is almost as old as the town itself. The design of the cemetery was
influenced by the Rural Cemetery movement which resulted in a wooded, park-like design.
(Source: Town of Winchester Official Website)
Sandy Beach permits swimming on the Upper Mystic Lake is controlled by the Department of

Conservation and Recreation. The Tricommunity Bikeway is a public, marked bike path which
follows the course of the Aberjona River, from the Woburn line to the Mystic Lakes. The
Middlesex Fells Reservation, 300 acres of woodland abutting the town on the eastern side, offers
miles of woods and trails and bridle paths, as well as Long Pond where ice-skating and nature
walks are available. The Upper Mystic Lake offers fishing and non-power boating.
(Source: Winchester League of Women Voters)

Winchester has no designated Areas of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC).

4.G.  ENVIRONMENTAL CHALLENGES
Winchester shares similar environmental problems with many urbanized
Massachusetts communities which have been the sites of agriculture and industry since the
1600's. The courses of rivers and streams have been altered, and ponds and wetlands have been
filled.

Studies by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Aberjona River Watershed Study
Group have identified chemicals in the sediment of the Aberjona River and the Mystic Lakes,
including arsenic, chromium and cadmium. The spread of these chemicals and their effects on
human health and the environment have been investigated by the Environmental Protection
Agency. EPA's Aberjona River Study Ecological Risk Assessment, dated September 2004,
included sampling sites in Winchester. Two sites, both in the Upper Mystic Lake, were shown to
pose a potential risk to the benthic invertebrate community.

4.G.2.  Landfills
Winchester has a closed landfill at McKay Avenue and uses a transfer station at the same
location to transport waste to a regional incinerator. The town maintains a composting area at the
transfer station.
4.G.3.  Erosion
Winchester has no significant erosion problems affecting wetlands or surface water.
4.G.4.  Flooding
Winchester has a flooding problem and has taken steps to mitigate flood impacts with a flood
study and implementation program.  The town has widened culverts and has invested in the latest
technology for stormwater management. The Center Falls Dam has been upgraded, culverts have
been added at Mount Vernon Street, Cross Street, Swanton Street and under the railroad line
behind the Muraco School. Two new culverts have been added under Skillings Field at the high
school.

4.G.5.  Sedimentation
River sedimentation continues to be a problem at various places with the Aberjona, River,
principally at Davidson Park, Judkins Pond Mill Pond.  Wedge Pond sediment flowing in from
Horn Pond Brook, and the Upper Mystic Lake has sand deltas formed from sand carried in by
stormwater pipe discharges.

Winchester is a mature suburban community, now increasing in density, as smaller homes are
demolished and replaced with larger structures.  Lots that formerly contained one home have
been subdivided and now contain several.  The Pansy Patch, former farmland, now contains
townhouses, and a portion of Wright Locke farm may soon be developed.  Preservation of open
space is of major importance to maintain the quality of life and to mitigate the impact that
development can have on local and regional flooding.  The Master Plan calls for greater density
of development in the downtown and in the MBTA 3A Districts.
4.G.7 Ground, Surface Water Pollution and Impaired Water Bodies
The Department of Environmental Protection lists the Aberjona River as an impaired water body
and the Water Resources Commission has listed it as having a highly stressed basin.
Contaminants include unionized ammonia, phosphorus, chloride, low dissolved oxygen and
pathogens, as well as contaminated sediment caused by old industrial practices. In addition,
Upper Mystic Lake, Wedge Pond, and Winter Pond are also listed as having impairments.

The bacterial contamination appears to be coming from the Aberjona River, as high bacteria

The Aberjona's watershed in town and upstream is highly urbanized and contributes untreated
stormwater into the river. All towns within the watershed are required to implement NPDES
Phase II Stormwater regulations.  (Of recent note is an extensive stormwater structure at McCall
School field.) The town has acquired land along the river for parkland and in 2003 passed a
revised Floodplain District bylaw.
When issuing permits, the Conservation Commission requires compliance with the state's
Stormwater Management Plan and Winchester's Stormwater Guidelines.  As a part of the
NPDES Phase II requirement, the Engineering Department oversees water quality best
management practices throughout town, and stormwater regulations have been updated to
provide for greater pollution attenuation.
Winchester has made considerable progress repairing and replacing sanitary sewerage structures
with a major sewer siphon near the Wedgemere Train Station and repairing overflows at Everett
Avenue and in several locations on the west side, ending what had been frequent point sources
for pollution.  The town is expanding the use of bio-swales and bio-retention ponds, rain gardens
and other landscape-oriented solutions to improve water quality.  In addition, the town is
installing infiltration trenches, which are a cost-effective approach to reducing phosphorus
pollution.

Finally, water within the Middlesex Fells reservoirs is treated by a water filtration plant. This
brings the town into compliance with the Surface Water Treatment Rule, a regulation
promulgated under the federal Safe Drinking Water Act.
Of recent discussion is the amount of impervious surface within the watershed.  The town is
currently examining possibilities to replace impervious with pervious surfaces.
4.G.8.  Invasive Plant Species
Winchester's waterways suffer from invasive plants. Oriental bittersweet lines the banks of the
Aberjona River. Purple loosestrife continues to be a problem. However, eradication has been
progressing at Locke Farm Pond, and Winter Pond, due to the release of loosestrife eating
beetles and an active neighborhood group, Friends of Winter Pond.  Other invasive species,
including garlic mustard, buckthorn and Norway Maple and knotweed have established
themselves in uplands, including conservation land, along river and stream corridors and on
private property.  Algae growth needs constant attention in the Mystic Lakes and Winter Pond.
At each annual Aberjona River Day, teams of volunteers clear sections of the riverbank of
invasive species.

SECTION 6 – COMMUNITY VISION
6.A.  DESCIPTION OF PROCESS
This Plan notes accomplishments from the 2013 Open Space and Recreation Plan and builds on
them.  Goals are influenced by recent land acquisitions, the town's Master Plan, floodplain
requirements, stormwater management requirements, climate change, and wildlife habitat
requirements.  Since the last Open Space and Recreation Plan (OSRP), there have been several
key steps the town has taken in its overall planning that contribute in some way to the OSRP.

sections.section_title: The most influential is the Winchester Master Plan 2030 Action Plan adopted in March 2020.
sections.content:
The town also developed an Athletic Fields Master Plan in May 2019 and an All-Hazards
Mitigation Plan in 2023.  Using these plans and other information, a draft update of the OSRP is
prepared by the Open Space and Recreation Plan Committee. The draft document is reviewed by
the Open Space and Recreation Committee, town departments, boards and committees.  The final
draft plan is distributed for public comment, and a public hearing is held. The final draft of each
Plan reflects the results of a public hearing.
6.B.  STATEMENT OF OPEN SPACE AND RECREATION GOALS
The OSRP seeks to promote the revitalization of fields, parks, waterways, conservation areas and
other green spaces, to enhance environmental quality, and to improve connections to neighboring
towns and stakeholders within the Aberjona River watershed.
We envision a sustainable town, resilient to the impacts of climate change, providing a healthy,
enriching environment for its citizens to enhance quality of life as well as protecting and
preserving the environment for future generations.  Open spaces and town facilities should be
accessible to all.
Achieving this vision includes:
• Increasing the quantity, and improving the quality, of athletic fields and other recreation
facilities
• Protecting and utilizing the remaining large tracts of land in Town that are currently
unprotected
• Continuing to acquire and/or protect land for conservation, flood storage, and water
supply protection
• Improving transparency and communication between departments and the community on
open space and recreation issues

The town encourages the use of conservation restrictions on private land, with several
conservation restrictions existing and noted in Section 5.
Some of Winchester's Open Space is managed by the Massachusetts Department of

sections.section_title: Conservation and Recreation, some by the Town of Winchester, and some is in private hands.
sections.content:
We seek to coordinate this state-municipal-private dynamic as efficiently as possible.
Since the 2013 Open Space and Recreation Plan, two large parcels have been acquired -
Winning Farm and Wright-Locke Farm.  Winning Farm is in the process of submitting a
Conservation Restriction, and Wright-Locke farm is an operating farm, which contains a
conservation restriction.  Wright-Locke Farm conservation area is adjacent to Whipple Hill, and
it is important to maintain the continuity of open space and wildlife corridor.

sections.section_title: At present, there are plans to acquire 16 forested acres along the Aberjona River at the
sections.content:
Winchester/Woburn town line from Montvale Land LLC.  This property is important as a
replacement for Well Field taken during the construction of the new Lynch Elementary School
and potentially as an area for flood storage.  In addition, it serves as an important wildlife
corridor.  If improved with trails and management of invasive species, it could provide a new
area for passive recreation.
Another large parcel of land is approximately 13 acres on Forest Cir. and No. Border Road,
owned by the Shannon Realty Trust.  This property contains a large wetland area (4 acres off No.

Border Rd.) that abuts Middlesex Fells.  It is an important part of the wildlife corridor between
Middlesex Fells and the Aberjona River.
Both properties are currently zone RDB, which if developed, could result in relatively highdensity housing, putting a strain on town services in these areas as well as increasing the risk of
flooding, decreasing wildlife habitat, and presenting other environmental concerns.

7.B. 1 PARKS AND OPEN SPACE PROXIMITY TO RESIDENCES
The town's 1924 Master Plan for Recreation Areas set goal to provide a playfield or small play
lot within 1⁄4 of a mile (about a five-minute walk) to every dwelling in Winchester. This goal was
reiterated in the town's 1953 Master Plan. Based on the spatial analysis shown below, almost all
of Winchester's residential parcels are within 1⁄4 of a mile from protected open space or outdoor
recreation land. The few parcels that fall outside of this radius are indicated in red on the map
below and are not in environmental justice communities.
7.B.2.  PUBLIC ACCESS and ACCESSIBILITY
Although the Tri-Community Greenway increases bike and pedestrian access to many parks and
athletic fields, including Ginn Field, Skillings Field, and the fields at Muraco School, other open
space and recreational land can be difficult to access by non-car transportation. There have been
recent examples of new development that has incorporated conservation areas into the site plan,
such as the recent Winning Farm development. This model can be followed to continue to
preserve open space within a developable site while accommodating future growth and make
open space sites more accessible by foot or by bike. In addition, there is limited or no parking at
many of the conservation spaces, limiting their use by residents not living in the immediate area.

One of the goals of the Open Space and Recreation Plan is "Universal Access", that is, access to
all, regardless of degree of mental or physical ability. These concepts should be incorporated into
the design of all facilities in town, whether new construction or rehabilitation of existing
facilities. The ADA Accessibility Assessment was completed in 2019 and is included in Section
12.  It should be noted here that all playground and field renovations since the last Open Space
and Recreation Plan have complied with current standards of accessibility.  Future renovations
will comply with the recommendations in the ADA Accessibility Assessment. In addition, the
bike path running along the Aberjona River is wheelchair accessible, and there is a wheelchair
accessible trail at Winning Farm.  However, conservation areas are lands in their natural
condition and do not provide universal accessibility.
7.B.3.  ABERJONA RIVER AND HORN POND BROOK FLOOD MANAGEMENT
Numerous storms since 1996 left Winchester with extensive flooding, causing health risks, safety
issues and ecological degradation, and exposed the need for greater flood control, both in
Winchester and in upstream and downstream communities.  The town commissioned flood
studies for the town, flood control projects have been constructed, and a significant portion of the
flood control remedies have been accomplished.    As the Aberjona River serves as Winchester's
most significant element of open space, its restoration and rehabilitation continue to be one of the
town's highest priorities.  All permits incorporate a river way plan, with landscaped banks, and
actions preserve or create wildlife habitat. Winchester has implemented a floodplain bylaw,
established a floodplain overlay district, and is vigorous in review of stormwater management for
all new construction.

sections.section_title: Like other urbanized suburban communities, much of the Town’s original forestland and
sections.content:
agricultural land has been developed--only 15 percent of the Town's total land area is
permanently protected open space under federal, state, or local jurisdiction. Winchester is largely
built out already making it unlikely that the Town's open space will increase substantially
beyond its current inventory. The challenge will be to preserve the quality of the Town's existing
open space--particularly as development and redevelopment pressures will increase density in
many areas of town. Many survey participants expressed concerns over the lack of natural open
space and noted that many of Winchester's open space sites are highly programmed, such as
recreational fields, agricultural land, parks, or cemeteries. Survey participants also were
concerned for the stewardship of Winchester's existing natural resources, raising issues of
sustainability, hydrology, and ecology.

The need to manage conservation areas and waterways is ongoing. The spread of non-native
plants chokes wetlands and trees and outcompetes native species.  Safety is a concern.  The
Commission has developed a land stewards' program, in which volunteers walk designated
conservation areas, take care of small problems, and report larger ones to the Commission.  They
perform minor tree and shrub pruning and clear and mark trails.  Heavier work is performed by
the Dept of Public Works or contracted to professional landscapers. The town needs to survey
areas where invasive plants are at their worst and make a plan to control their spread.  This
project is currently underway with an Audubon baseline study of conservation and other forested
areas.

The Conservation Commission has a habitat protection and replacement program, and the town
has established the Peter Van Aken tree fund and the Street Tree Committee, which replace trees
in public areas throughout town.  Conservation areas should be managed to address the effect of
climate change on plants and wildlife.

Trees are a vital part of the natural resources of Conservation Spaces.  As the longest-lived
species, they are the foundation of the ecosystem and need to be protected.  Trees contribute to
their environment by providing oxygen, improving air quality, climate amelioration, conserving
water, preserving soil, and supporting wildlife.

Forest ecosystems will face direct and indirect impacts from climate changes.  Various tree
species may be more greatly impacted than others.  Model projections suggest that many
northern and boreal species, including balsam fir, red spruce, and black spruce may fare worse
under future conditions, but other species may benefit from projected changes in climate.  In
addition, non-native pests may make targeted tree species especially vulnerable.

sections.section_title: Conservation strategies for forested habitats to increase resilience to climate change include
sections.content:
diversifying the age structure and species composition of the forested landscape, controlling
white-tailed deer densities, and controlling invasive plant species and non-native pests by
detecting and tracking infestations and outbreaks in their early stages, and taking aggressive
actions to eliminate these problems before they escape control.  The Conservation Commission is
developing a Forest Stewardship Plan for the Winchester Town Forest, an effort which will be
applied to all large, forested conservation areas in the future.
7.B.6.  PROTECTION FROM EXTREME HEAT

sections.section_title: As daytime temperatures increase due to climate change, protection from extreme heat will
sections.content:
become important.  In the Wicked Hot Mystic model developed by the Mystic River Watershed
Association, the hottest areas in Winchester are in the middle of town and along the Main Street
corridor north of town. Preserving open space and increasing tree canopy in these areas can
decrease the risk of extreme heat.
Open spaces and recreation areas that provide opportunities for cooling recreation activities such
as swimming are important to heat resilience. Borggaard Beach on Wedge Pond is closed
permanently due to lack of staffing and Shannon Beach on Upper Mystic Lake was closed a
large percentage of the time in the summer of 2023 due to bacterial contamination.  It is
important to keep this facility open as much as possible.

7.B.7 CLIMATE CHANGE, OPEN SPACE, AND PUBLIC HEALTH
The Winchester Board of Health recognizes that Winchester's open spaces and recreational areas
are public health assets and as such deserve Town protection, enhancement and expansion where
possible.

The intersection of public health, climate change1 and safe outdoor recreation has become even
more apparent since Covid 19 appeared and since local climate change impacts have accelerated
in recent years.
Observations from a private resident include the paragraphs below:

sections.section_title: The town is experiencing growth in populations of both young and older residents2. These two
sections.content:
groups are particularly vulnerable to some public health impacts of climate change such as
extreme heat and cold, poor air quality, ice and windstorms, certain pests such as ticks3 and
mosquitos, along with the increasing recognition that climate change stress and anxiety is a
public health risk4. Encouragingly however, taking action to support the most vulnerable
populations' access to open space and recreation will have positive impacts for all residents,
workers and visitors to Winchester.
That long-feared climate risk to Winchester's open spaces crept significantly closer in 2024,
with multiple simultaneous brush fires spreading across many communities on the North Shore,
destroying acres of shrubbery and trees and creating air quality impacts beyond the

municipalities where the fires started. Repeated droughts plus the spread of plant pests due to
milder winters are turning our open spaces into potential tinder boxes. Droughts also reduce the
availability of supplementary water sources, such as ponds and streams, to fight fires in remote
areas. The occurrence of high winds with wildfires increases the risk of multiple simultaneous
fires regionally and poses a new urgency to protect Winchester's open spaces in every way
possible.

cold, fire, plant and animal pests and more. Open space and recreation will play an important

7.B.8  Private Efforts (From Swim Winchester)
There is currently no indoor community pool in the Town of Winchester. Over the last 50 years,
there have been multiple efforts to build one. The latest effort is organized by Swim Winchester
(https://swimwinchester.org), a 501(c)(3) non-profit established in 2014 with the goal to build a
community aquatic facility that will be a resource for community members of all ages for
recreation, training, water safety and aquatic fitness classes, wellness, rehabilitation/special
needs and public events. In 2018, the Select Board and School Committee granted conditional
approval of a site in the northeast corner of Skillings Field for the pool. Swim Winchester has
worked with consultants and the Town to study the site and hired an architectural firm to develop
a preliminary design for the facility that includes two swimming pools (a lap pool and a
recreation pool) along with fitness space. Design plans incorporate sustainability measures
addressing, among other areas: energy efficiency, indoor/outdoor air quality, and water
consumption. Swim Winchester is in the early stages of a capital campaign to raise funds to build
the pool and is working with the Town on the steps needed to obtain construction permits and
approvals.
7.B.9 IMPROVE WATER QUALITY
The major water bodies in Winchester, Aberjona River, Upper Mystic Lake, Wedge Pond, and
Winter Pond all have water quality impairments that can limit their use for recreation.  These
impairments have impacts on the users of these resources, including health risks to those who
swim, boat, or fish in these waters, risks to pets, and impacts on wildlife in and around these
waters.  Shannon Beach, the only swimming area in Winchester, was closed for a significant
number of days during 2023 due to high bacterial levels.
Winchester has a Stormwater Management Plan to decrease pollutants coming from stormwater
run-off, namely bacteria and phosphorus.  Additional work needs to be done to identify and
decrease or eliminate sources of pollution and potentially treat pond waters to decrease
phosphorus.

The Conservation Commission has always strived to inform the public of environmental issues

7.D.  OPEN SPACE AND RECREATION NEEDS WITHIN A REGIONAL
CONTEXT (From the 2017 Massachusetts Comprehensive Outdoor and Recreation

Winchester lies within the highly urbanized metropolitan Boston region, home to 1.9 million
people, almost one-third (31%) of the state's total population.  To the north, the Middlesex Fells
Reservation incorporates a rim of the Boston harbor basin, and is part of a regional park system
that, through river corridors, seeks to preserve open space to the sea. Future open space and
recreation projects will need to take the need to enhance these connections into consideration.

7.D.1.  Ownership and Management of Open Space Lands
Some of Winchester's open spaces are managed by the Department of Conservation and
Recreation, some by the Town of Winchester, and some is in private hands.  We seek to
coordinate this state-municipal-private dynamic as efficiently as possible.
7.D.2.  Opinion Survey for services in Massachusetts SCORP 2017
The most desired services in the Massachusetts SCORP Survey are bike paths, hiking/walking
trails, and playgrounds for 2- to 5-year-olds, and playgrounds for those with disabilities (see
graphic below).
The report cites the highest funding priorities for municipalities over the next five years include
playgrounds, ballfields (soccer, lacrosse, baseball, etc.), community or regional trail systems, and
improved pedestrian access to parks (sidewalks, safe road crossings, etc.).  The need to invest
more in trails and pedestrian access corresponds with the increase in popularity identified by the
survey takers over the past five to 10 years in walking, trails, and hiking by their constituents.
Municipalities also identified walking, rail trails, biking, and hiking as the activities they believe
will increase in popularity over the next five years.  When asked what facilities are not currently
available in a community, but should be, trails and bicycling facilities top the list.

The Open Space and Recreation Plan encourages the use and maintenance of all open space and
recreational facilities through funding for regular maintenance.  It also seeks to develop a
network of open spaces by increasing land under conservation, improving habitat, and
developing more areas as actively used green spaces.
Specific goals are described below.
8.A Goal: Increase participation and resources for conservation and stewardship
The Winchester Conservation Commission is responsible for the management and protection of
almost 150 acres of permanently protected areas of natural open space known as Conservation

sections.section_title: Areas. The purpose of these Conservation Areas is for the protection of natural resources and
sections.content:
providing opportunities to the public for passive recreational activities.
Conservation Areas are monitored and maintained, in part, through the work of volunteers.
However, Conservations Areas need more resources than are currently available.
In addition, the Conservation Commission promotes involvement of residents in stewardship of
our Conservation Areas to give back to the community and promote a healthy environment.

8.B Goal: Improve user experience in Conservation Areas
Conservation Areas are maintained through the efforts of Winchester Land Stewards, Scouts,
volunteers, and the Department of Public Works.  However, many of our Conservation Areas are
in need of additional improvement and restoration that will improve the experience of visitors.
We look to establish a Conservation Lands Interest Group, comprised from public and private
entities, which would give a broad perspective on needs and suggestions.
8.C. Goal: Improve Accessibility in Conservation Areas and Open Spaces
One of the goals of the Open Space and Recreation Plan is "Universal Access", that is, access to
all, regardless of degree of mental or physical ability.  There currently are accessible areas within
our Conservation Areas and Open Spaces including the bike path running along the Aberjona
River, and there is a wheelchair accessible trail at Winning Farm.
8.D. Goal: Protect and restore Conservation Areas and Great Ponds
Winning Farm, a newly acquired property, requires restoration to meet its potential as a
recreation area. Winchester's Great Ponds are also in need of water quality improvement. As
climate change progresses, an overall increase in temperatures may cause damage to water
bodies and open spaces.  Protection of these resources will preserve wildlife habitat and will
increase the quality of life by providing recreation, environmental improvement, and increased
resilience to climate change by providing flood storage, carbon sequestration, and decreasing risk
of extreme heat.

The Town’s 2020 Climate Action Plan describes an overall strategy to reduce carbon pollution (a
leading cause of climate change) by 80% in 2050 and describes specific measures to enhance our
community's resilience to the impacts of climate change.
https://www.winchester.us/documentcenter/view/4622 . Increased tree planting and water quality
improvements will aid in cooling temperatures, preventing flooding, improving wildlife habitat,
and improving quality of life

NOTICE UNDER THE AMERICANS WITH DISABILITIES ACT

In accordance with the requirements of Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990
(ADA), the Town of Winchester will not discriminate against individuals with disabilities on the
basis of disability in its services, programs or activities.
Employment: The Town of Winchester does not discriminate on the basis of disability in its
hiring or employment practices and complies with all regulations promulgated by the U.S. Equal
Employment Opportunity Commission under Title I of the ADA.
Effective Communication: The Town of Winchester will generally, upon request, provide aids
and services leading to effective communication for qualified persons with disabilities so they
can participate equally in the Town of Winchester's programs, services and activities, including
qualified sign language interpreters, documents in Braille, and other ways of making information
and communications accessible to people who have speech, hearing or vision impairments.
Modification to Policies and Procedures: The Town of Winchester will make all reasonable
modifications to policies and programs to ensure that people with disabilities have an equal
opportunity to enjoy all of its programs, services and activities.
Anyone who requires auxiliary aid or service for effective communication, or a modification of
policies or procedures to participate in a program, service or activity of the Town of Winchester,
should contact the office of the ADA Coordinator as soon as possible but no later than five
business days before the scheduled event.
The Town of Winchester will not place a surcharge on a particular individual with a disability
or any group of individuals with disabilities to cover the cost of providing auxiliary aid/services
or reasonable modifications of policies or procedures, such as retrieving items from locations
that are open to the public but are not accessible to persons who use wheelchairs.
The ADA does not require the Town of Winchester to take any action that would fundamentally
alter the nature of its programs or services or impose an undue financial or administrative
burden.
Complaints that a program, services, or activity of the Town of Winchester is not accessible to
persons with disabilities should be directed to the Anne Graglia-Kostos, ADA Coordinator,
